01.note: Mar Zutra was visiting Rav Ashi's home when a death struck the household and Rav Ashi was in mourning. Mar Zutra recited one long combined blessing: it opened with "Who is good and does good," went on to praise God as the true Judge who takes away with justice and does in His world as He wills, and closed with a prayer that God, who repairs the breaches in Israel, repair this breach for life.
01.why: The Gemara has just read a baraita about what is said in a house of mourning and concluded that "Who is good and does good" is said there as well as "the true Judge." Mar Zutra's blessing shows both said together.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A Sage who happened to visit Rav Ashi's home and recited the blessing.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage in whose home the death occurred.

terms.term: Who is good and does good
terms.meaning: A blessing thanking God for good; it is also the fourth blessing of Grace after Meals.
A blessing said on hearing of a death, accepting God's judgment as just.

02.note: Rav and Rabbi Hiyya were eating a meal in the presence of Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi). Rabbi told Rav: "Stand, wash your hands." Rabbi Hiyya saw that Rav was trembling, afraid he had done something wrong at the meal. Rabbi Hiyya reassured him: "Son of noblemen, he is telling you to review Grace after Meals," since the first to wash at the end of a meal would be the one to lead the blessing.
02.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav's rule that whoever washes his hands first at the end of a meal leads Grace after Meals; this meal shows that practice in action.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage dining before Rabbi, told to wash his hands.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage at the same meal who explained Rabbi's instruction to Rav.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the host before whom they ate.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

03.note: Ravin and Abaye were riding along a road. Ravin's donkey went ahead of Abaye's, and Ravin did not say "Let the Master go first." Abaye said to himself that since Ravin came up from the Land of Israel he had become arrogant. But at the door of the synagogue Ravin said, "Let the Master enter." Abaye asked, "Until now was I not Master?" Ravin answered that Rabbi Yohanan taught one defers to a greater person only at a doorway that has a mezuza.
03.why: The Sages have just taught that one does not show deference on roads or bridges; this journey illustrates the rule, and the Gemara goes on to refine Rabbi Yohanan's "mezuza" wording.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: A Sage who had come from the Land of Israel; he rode ahead and later deferred at the synagogue door.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage traveling with Ravin who thought him arrogant.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Ravin quoted.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with Torah verses fixed to the doorpost of a home.
A Babylonian way of referring to the Land of Israel.

04.note: Rav and Shmuel were sitting at a meal when Rav Shimi bar Hiyya arrived late and began eating in a hurry. Rav asked him why he was rushing: to join them for the zimmun? They had already eaten. Shmuel answered Rav that they had not really finished: if someone brought truffles or a young pigeon for Rav, would they not eat it?
04.why: The discussion turns back to the zimmun; the exchange asks whether a latecomer can join diners who have stopped eating, and Shmuel's answer is that they are still in their meal while they would still eat more.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage at the meal; Shmuel calls him Abba.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage at the meal who argued they had not yet finished.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
people.about: A latecomer who hurried to eat.

terms.meaning: The invitation to say Grace after Meals together, recited when at least three people have eaten as a group; one person leads and the others respond.

05.note: Rami bar Hama would not include Rav Menashya bar Tahlifa in a zimmun, although Rav Menashya had studied Sifra, Sifrei and halakhot. When Rami bar Hama died, Rava said he died only because he had refused to include Rav Menashya. The Gemara asks why, given the teaching that one who studied but did not serve Torah scholars is an am ha'aretz, and answers that Rav Menashya had served the Sages; Rami bar Hama simply did not check carefully.
05.why: The Gemara has just listed opinions on who counts as an am ha'aretz, who may not be included in a zimmun, and Rav Huna ruled like the opinion that even one who studied but did not serve scholars is one. This case tests that ruling.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: A Sage who refused to include Rav Menashya bar Tahlifa in a zimmun, and died.

people.name: Rav Menashya bar Tahlifa
people.about: A scholar of Sifra, Sifrei and halakhot who, the Gemara says, had served the Sages.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who said Rami bar Hama died because of this.

terms.meaning: The invitation to say Grace after Meals together, recited when at least three people have eaten as a group; one person leads and the others respond.
Literally "people of the land": someone not careful in religious law or learning; the Sages debate the exact definition.
Early collections of the Sages' interpretations of the books of Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy.

06.note: When Abaye and Rava were children they sat before Rabba, who asked them, "To whom does one recite blessings?" They answered, "To the All-Merciful." He asked, "And where does the All-Merciful reside?" Rava pointed to the ceiling; Abaye went outside and pointed toward the sky. Rabba told them, "You will both become Sages," quoting the saying that a cucumber can be recognized from its blossom.
06.why: The Gemara has just ruled, following Rav Nahman, that a minor who knows to Whom one blesses is included in a zimmun; this scene shows children being tested on exactly that.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: As a child, he went outside and pointed to the sky.

people.name: Rava
people.about: As a child, he pointed to the ceiling.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The teacher who questioned the two boys.

terms.meaning: A common Aramaic name for God.

07.note: King Yannai and his queen were eating together, but since Yannai had killed the Sages there was no one to lead Grace after Meals. The queen made him swear not to harm the man she brought, then brought her brother Shimon ben Shatah and seated him between them. Yannai boasted of the honor he gave him; Shimon replied that the Torah honors him, not the king, and Yannai complained that he does not accept authority. Given a cup to bless over, Shimon asked how he could say "from Whom Yannai and his companions have eaten" when he had eaten nothing. He drank that cup, was given another, and recited the blessing.
07.why: The Gemara has been asking how much and what kind of food one must eat to join a zimmun; right after, Rabbi Yohanan says Shimon ben Shatah acted on his own, since one cannot lead others in Grace without eating an olive's bulk of grain.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: The king who had killed the Sages and needed someone to lead Grace after Meals.

people.name: the queen
people.about: Yannai's wife and Shimon ben Shatah's sister, who brought him under oath.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: The queen's brother, a Sage, who led the blessing.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.
A cup of wine held by the leader while reciting Grace after Meals.

08.note: Rabbi Zeira invited Rav Hisda to come and teach. Rav Hisda refused: he had not yet learned Grace after Meals, so how could he teach? He explained that at the Exilarch's house he had led Grace, and Rav Sheshet stiffened his neck at him like a snake because he left out covenant, Torah and sovereignty. He had followed Rav's view that omitting them is acceptable, since covenant does not apply to women, and Torah and sovereignty apply neither to women nor slaves. Rabbi Zeira answered: you abandoned all those other Sages and followed Rav?
08.why: The Gemara is working out what each blessing of Grace after Meals must contain and how it ends; this exchange shows that leaving covenant, Torah and sovereignty out of the second blessing drew a sharp rebuke.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage who invited Rav Hisda to teach and criticized his choice.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage who led Grace at the Exilarch's house and was rebuked.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: The Sage who angrily challenged Rav Hisda's blessing.

terms.meaning: The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
Themes traditionally mentioned in Grace: the covenant of circumcision, the gift of the Torah, and the kingdom of David.

09.note: Giddel bar Manyumi was standing before Rav Nahman when Rav Nahman forgot the special Shabbat passage in Grace after Meals and went back to the beginning to say it all again. Giddel asked why he did that. Rav Nahman answered that Rabbi Sheila taught in Rav's name: one who errs goes back to the beginning.
09.why: Just before, Rav Giddel taught in Rav's name a short blessing for one who forgot Shabbat. Rav Nahman's conduct contradicts that, and the Gemara next resolves it: the short blessing works only before starting "Who is good and does good."

people.name: Giddel bar Manyumi
people.about: He saw Rav Nahman restart Grace and asked why.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who forgot the Shabbat passage and started Grace over.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

10.note: Ravina and Rav Hama bar Buzi were at a meal at the Exilarch's house. At the end, Rav Hama got up and went around looking to gather a hundred people so the zimmun for a hundred could be said. Ravina told him there was no need, because Rava had ruled like Rabbi Akiva.
10.why: The Mishna gives two views: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says the zimmun wording grows with the size of the crowd; Rabbi Akiva says it stays the same once there are ten. Rava rules like Rabbi Akiva, and this scene shows that ruling applied.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who told Rav Hama not to bother gathering a hundred.

people.name: Rav Hama bar Buzi
people.about: A Sage who tried to gather a hundred diners.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Ravina quoted.

terms.meaning: The invitation to say Grace after Meals together, recited when at least three people have eaten as a group; one person leads and the others respond.
The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

11.note: Rafram bar Pappa came to the synagogue of Abei Givar and was called to read from the Torah. He said "Bless the Lord" and stopped, without adding "the blessed One." The whole congregation cried out "Bless the Lord the blessed One." Rava said to him: "You black pot, why get involved in a dispute? Besides, the common practice follows Rabbi Yishmael."
11.why: The Mishna records Rabbi Akiva's call "Bless the Lord" against Rabbi Yishmael's "Bless the Lord the blessed One." Rava has ruled like Rabbi Akiva for the zimmun, yet here he says synagogue practice follows Rabbi Yishmael.

people.name: Rafram bar Pappa
people.about: A Sage who used the shorter call to bless before reading the Torah.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who told him practice follows Rabbi Yishmael.

terms.meaning: An affectionate nickname for a Torah scholar who works hard at study.
The call to the congregation before reading the Torah; the congregation answers with a blessing.

12.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were eating together when dates and pomegranates were brought. Mar Zutra tossed some fruit to Rav Ashi. Rav Ashi asked him whether he did not hold that one may not throw food. Mar Zutra said that rule was about bread. Rav Ashi quoted a teaching that, like bread, other foods may not be thrown; Mar Zutra answered with another teaching that bread may not be thrown but other foods may.
12.why: The Sages have just listed ways to show respect for bread, including not throwing it. This meal asks whether the rule covers other food, and the Gemara reconciles the two teachings: food that gets spoiled by throwing may not be thrown.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage eating with Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: He tossed fruit to Rav Ashi and defended it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: He objected that food may not be thrown.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages of the Mishna's era that was not included in the Mishna itself.

13.note: After Ulla refused to send the cup of blessing to Rav Nahman's wife Yalta, quoting a teaching that a woman is blessed through her husband, Yalta heard. She rose in a rage, went into the wine store and broke four hundred barrels of wine. Rav Nahman asked Ulla to send her another cup. Ulla sent one with the message that all the wine in that barrel was wine of blessing. She sent back: "From peddlers come words, and from rags come lice."
13.why: The Gemara has been listing the practices for the cup of blessing, including sending it to one's household so the wife is blessed; this incident tests that practice.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Nahman's wife, daughter of the Exilarch, who broke the wine barrels in anger.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Yalta's husband and Ulla's host.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A guest who led Grace and would not send Yalta the cup.

terms.meaning: A cup of wine held by the leader while reciting Grace after Meals.

13.flag: The STORY starts with a baraita of Rabbi Natan and misses the opening of the incident (Ulla's visit and refusal), which sits in the BEFORE segment just above.

14.note: Two students ate and did not say Grace. One forgot by accident, and following Beit Shammai he went back to where he had eaten, and found a purse of gold. The other skipped it on purpose and, following Beit Hillel, did not go back, and a lion ate him.
14.why: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree over whether one who forgot Grace must return to where he ate, and the Gemara has just said that even Beit Hillel require a return when it was skipped on purpose. The two students show the results.

terms.meaning: The schools of two early Sages, Shammai and Hillel, who often disagreed on Jewish law.
The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

15.note: Rabba bar bar Hana was traveling with a caravan when he ate and forgot to say Grace. He thought: if I tell them I forgot to bless, they will tell me to bless here, since God can be blessed anywhere. Better to say I forgot a golden dove. He told them to wait for him because he had forgotten a golden dove, went back, said the blessing, and found a golden dove.
15.why: The discussion is about whether one who forgot Grace must go back to where he ate, as Beit Shammai hold; this journey follows the two students who went back, or did not, with their rewards.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage traveling with a caravan who went back to say Grace.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

16.note: A man was walking along the right side of the Euphrates when a lion attacked him. A miracle happened and he was saved. He came to Rava, who told him: every time you reach that place, say the blessing "Blessed... Who performed a miracle for me in this place."
16.why: Rabbi Yohanan has derived from Jethro's words that one blesses God for a miracle. The Gemara asks whether that applies only to a miracle for the many, and brings this case to show an individual blesses too.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who told the rescued man which blessing to say.

17.note: Mar, son of Ravina, was walking in the marketplace of Mehoza when a wild camel attacked him. The wall split open, he went inside it, and was saved. After that, at the willows (where a spring had once appeared for him when he was thirsty) he would bless God "Who performed a miracle for me in the willows and with the camel," and at the Mehoza market, "with the camel and in the willows."
17.why: The Gemara asked whether one blesses for a miracle done for an individual; these cases show one does, and the Sages conclude that everyone blesses for a public miracle, but only the person himself for a private one.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Sage saved from a wild camel, who blessed God for it.

18.note: A noblewoman told Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi El'ai that his face looked like those of pig farmers and moneylenders, people who live well without hard work. He told her that both trades were forbidden to him. Rather, between his lodging and the study hall there were twenty-four bathrooms, and on his way he stopped to relieve himself in every one of them.
18.why: Rav Yehuda had praised lingering in the bathroom, and the Gemara has just distinguished healthy lingering from harmful straining. This anecdote shows the benefit.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi El'ai
people.about: A Sage whose healthy face a noblewoman commented on.

people.name: a matron
people.about: A noblewoman who remarked on his well-fed face.

terms.meaning: Moneylenders who charge interest, which the Torah forbids among Jews.

19.note: Rabbi Bena'a, passed down through a long chain of Sages, recalled that there were twenty-four dream interpreters in Jerusalem. He once had a dream and went to all of them. Each gave a different interpretation, and every one of them came true for him.
19.why: The discussion is about whether dreams are true or false; this account backs the saying that "all dreams follow the mouth" of the interpreter, which the Gemara then traces to a verse and limits.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: The elder who went to all twenty-four interpreters.

20.note: The Roman emperor challenged Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rabbi Hananya: you Jews say you are very wise, so tell me what I will see in my dream. Rabbi Yehoshua said he would see the Persians capture him, enslave him, and make him herd unclean animals with a golden staff. The emperor thought about it all day, and that night he dreamed it. Likewise King Shapur of Persia asked Shmuel, who said he would see the Romans take him captive and make him grind date pits in golden mills. He thought about it all day and that night he dreamed it.
20.why: Rabbi Yonatan has just taught that a person is shown in a dream only the thoughts of his heart; both rulers dream what they spent the day thinking about.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who challenged Rabbi Yehoshua.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rabbi Hananya
people.about: The Sage who foretold the emperor's dream.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: The king of Persia who challenged Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who foretold Shapur's dream.

terms.meaning: Animals the Torah forbids Jews to eat, such as pigs.
